wolf-vs-goat.types: Wolf vs Goat is not a grading system for wool. Treat it as an apparel brand that publishes educational product writing about fiber diameter, yarn brands and cloth construction. The useful types to track in its public stories are generic fiber classes (merino wool, linen, cotton, silk), mill yarn brands (for example Zegna Baruffa's Cashwool, described by the mill as about 19.5 micron extrafine merino), and mill fabric collections (for example Loro Piana's Pecora Nera naturally pigmented wool cloths). Those three layers answer different questions. Afromood, as the brand has described it, is a Filmar-spun linen and Egyptian cotton yarn rather than a wool grade, which makes it a clear example of a mill yarn name that is not a fiber class.
wolf-vs-goat.fabrics: Garments discussed in the brand's public materials include fully fashioned multi-ply merino cardigans, seamless knit sweaters in linen-cotton yarn, and tailored trousers in wool-silk-linen cloths. Construction details the brand emphasizes, such as ply count, fully fashioned knitting or pile weaves in other essays, belong to textile structure rather than to a proprietary fiber. Use those essays as practice for reading any maker's fabric story: separate the weave or knit, the yarn brand and the legal fiber percentages.
wolf-vs-goat.quality: When a brand teaches microns, ask for the number, the test basis and whether it refers to top, yarn or finished cloth. Cashwool's mill page states 19.5 micron extrafine merino; the brand's own cardigan story repeats that figure and adds a finishing claim about hand. Treat the finishing claim as producer language unless a test report is offered. For trousers, read the exact blend percentages on the label rather than the collection name alone. Prefer dense, even knitting, secure linking and honest blend disclosure over adjectives such as luxury or heirloom.
pros: Public product writing that names mill yarns and microns can train readers to ask better materials questions of any brand.
Attributed examples make the difference between fiber class and mill product tangible.
Construction notes such as ply count or fully fashioned knitting connect handfeel to structure, not only to fiber names.
Separating educational storytelling from certification keeps the limits of a brand entry clear.
cons: An apparel trademark does not standardize fiber quality across every SKU.
Producer stories can mix measured facts with marketing comparisons that lack a published test method.
Named mill yarns may change, go exclusive or be discontinued without any change in the generic fiber on a label.
This atlas does not verify factory lists, animal-welfare audits or batch-level traceability for the brand.
wolf-vs-goat.impact: Impact follows the fibers and processes in each garment: sheep farming and scouring for wool, flax or cotton agriculture for plant yarns, and dyeing and finishing energy in both cases. Naming an Italian mill does not by itself establish farm origin, land management or living-wage sewing. Undyed pigmented wool collections can avoid some dyeing steps for those shades, which is a process difference rather than a complete life-cycle claim. No brand-level life-cycle assessment is cited here. Readers should look for product-specific composition, care that extends wear life and any third-party wool or farm standards that actually cover the SKU.
wolf-vs-goat.care: Care is garment-specific. Follow the sewn-in label. Fine merino knits often prefer cool gentle washing with wool detergent free of protease enzymes, then flat drying; some pieces are dry clean only. Linen-cotton knits may have different dimensional change and wrinkle behavior than wool. Wool-silk-linen trousers are commonly dry clean only. Multi-ply dense knits still pill if abraded and still feed clothes moths if stored dirty. Air between wears, store clean and respect heat limits so you do not undo the construction quality the brand describes.
faq: Is Wolf vs Goat a type of wool?
No. It is an apparel brand. The wool in its garments is still generic wool or merino unless the label states a blend. Use the brand's writing to learn questions, then read each garment's fiber line.
What do Cashwool, Afromood and Pecora Nera mean in its stories?

They are mill yarn or cloth product names the brand has discussed publicly: Cashwool with Zegna Baruffa, Afromood with Filmar, and Pecora Nera with Loro Piana. They illustrate commercial product lines, not new generic fibers, and mentioning them here is not an endorsement.
Does a mill name tell me where the sheep were raised?

Not by itself. Merino is often grown in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa or South America and spun or woven in Europe. Ask for farm or country-of-origin evidence separately from the spinner's brand.
Why is this brand in a fiber atlas?

Because its public materials education is a convenient reference for practicing the same distinctions the atlas teaches: fiber class versus yarn brand versus cloth construction. The entry is referenceOnly and adds no map edges.
notable: Zegna Baruffa's public Cashwool description states extrafine merino at 19.5 microns; Wolf vs Goat's cardigan story attributes that yarn to its 10-ply knit.
The brand's Afromood sweater note describes a Filmar yarn as about 68 percent linen and 32 percent Egyptian cotton, a clear mill-yarn-versus-fiber-class teaching example.
Pecora Nera is presented in the brand's writing as a Loro Piana cloth using naturally dark New Zealand wool, sometimes blended with silk and linen in the brand's trousers.

canali.types: Canali is not a wool grade. Track three layers in menswear language: generic fiber (wool, silk, linen, elastane blends), cloth construction (twill, hopsack, fresco-like open weaves), and the garment house brand. Biella names a textile district. Super S numbers, when present on cloth tickets, are commercial cloth designations. Do not collapse house, district and fiber into one word.
canali.fabrics: Typical educational examples are tailored jackets and trousers in wool or wool-rich cloths associated with Italian menswear. Open high-twist tropical cloths and denser year-round suitings illustrate how weave and twist change seasonality. Use Canali product stories as practice for reading any maker’s cloth description, then verify the sewn-in label.
canali.quality: Prefer clear fiber percentages, cloth weight or season code, and honest blend disclosure over heritage adjectives alone. Check shoulder construction and pressing quality on the garment. If a cloth mill is named, treat that as an attributed supply detail for that SKU, not a permanent atlas edge.
pros: House and district language helps learners separate brand, place and fiber.
Tailoring vocabulary connects handfeel to weave and make, not only to fiber names.
Label-first reading habits transfer to any menswear brand.
referenceOnly framing keeps commercial prestige out of the science layer.
cons: A menswear trademark does not standardize every cloth across seasons.
Biella marketing can be mistaken for farm origin.
Public pages may omit micron or mill ticket details.
No atlas map edge should be invented from lookbooks.
canali.impact: Impact follows the fiber farming system, dyeing and finishing chemistry, garment transport and how long the suit stays in wear. A Biella make-up or design location does not by itself document farm practice or dyehouse standards. Prefer product-specific certifications when a seller offers them, and keep house marketing language separate from verified farm or chemical standards.
canali.care: Follow the garment care label without exception. Wool suiting often needs pressing and rest between wears; spot clean when possible. Steam carefully on fused or canvassed constructions so adhesives and canvases are not damaged. Store jackets on shaped hangers, brush cloth gently, and avoid crushing the shoulders in tight closets.
faq: Is Canali a type of wool?
No. Canali is a menswear house trademark. The fiber in a garment remains wool or whatever blend the sewn-in label states, independent of the house name on the jacket.
Does Biella on a page mean Italian sheep?
Not necessarily. Biella usually marks processing, design or menswear culture in northern Italy. The sheep that grew the wool may have been raised in another country entirely.
Why list Canali in a fiber atlas?
Because it is a useful reference brand for reading mill-district and tailoring language. The atlas is educational, not a supplier directory, and adds no commercial map edges for the house.
Are there map links for Canali mills?
No. This project does not invent mill-to-brand map edges. Cloth or mill names that appear in lookbooks stay as attributed text, not as atlas logistics routes.
notable: Educational focus: Biella menswear vocabulary versus generic fiber names.
No proprietary fiber chemistry is implied by the house trademark.
Cloth tickets and sewn-in labels remain the composition authority.
